title: Learning in public
translation: You hear it all the time from people who want to learn something: "I don't want anyone to know until I'm good at it. I'll practise on my own, and then I'll show up and impress everyone." People like that never learn a thing.

Go and join the people who are good while you're still terrible. Let them laugh at you and make fun of you, don't be embarrassed, just keep at it. Even with no talent at all, if you don't get stuck and don't get sloppy, over the years you'll get past the talented ones who never practise. In the end you're one of the best. People respect you, and you have a name like nobody else.

Even the best people in any field were terrible when they started, and everyone knew it. They had some awful flaws, too. But they took the rules of their craft seriously and didn't just do whatever they liked, and that's how they ended up as the ones everyone learns from. It's the same with music, with games, with anything.
original: {能|のう}をつかむとする{人|ひと}、「よくせざらむ{程|ほど}は、なまじひに{人|ひと}に{知|し}られじ、{内々|うちうち}よく{習|なら}ひ{得|え}てさし{出|い}でたらむこそ、いと{心|こころ}にくからめ。」と{常|つね}にいふめれど、かくいふ{人|ひと}、{一芸|いちげい}もならひ{得|う}ることなし。

いまだ{堅固|けんご}かたほなるより、{上手|じやうず}の{中|なか}にまじりて、{譏|そし}り{笑|わら}はるるにも{恥|は}ぢず、つれなくて{過|す}ぎてたしなむ{人|ひと}、{天性|てんせい}その{骨|こつ}なけれども、{道|みち}になづまず{妄|みだ}りにせずして、{年|とし}を{送|おく}れば、{堪能|かんのう}の{嗜|たしな}まざるよりは、{終|つひ}に{上手|じやうず}の{位|くらゐ}にいたり、{徳|とく}たけ{人|ひと}に{許|ゆる}されて、ならびなき{名|な}をうることなり。
{天下|てんか}の{物|もの}の{上手|じやうず}といへども、はじめは{不堪|ふかん}のきこえもあり、{無下|むげ}の{瑕瑾|かきん}もありき。
されどもその{人|ひと}、{道|みち}の{掟|おきて}{正|ただ}しく、これを{重|おも}くして{放埒|はうらつ}せざれば、{世|よ}の{博士|はかせ}にて、{万人|ばんにん}の{師|し}となること、{諸道|しよだう}かはるべからず。
literal: People who try to acquire a skill always seem to say, 'As long as I cannot do it well, I'd rather not, rashly, become known to people; to learn it well privately and then come forward would surely be very impressive', but people who say so do not learn even one art.

A person who, while still completely unskilled, mixes among the skilled, is not ashamed to be criticised and laughed at, and passes the time unbothered, practising: even if by nature he has no knack for it, if he does not stall on the way, does not act carelessly, and lets the years go by, he will finally reach the rank of a master, ahead of the talented person who does not practise, his authority will grow, he will be recognised by people, and he will win an unrivalled name.
Even the masters of the land at first had a reputation for being incompetent, and had terrible flaws too.

But because such a person keeps the rules of the way correctly, holds them important and does not act at will, he becomes an authority of the world and the teacher of all people: this cannot differ in any art.

notes.text: {能|のう}: any skill or art. (Noh theatre was only taking shape in Kenkō's time.) The original says 'a person who…' all the way through; the translation switches to 'you' for the advice.

{心|こころ}にくし: 'impressive, admirable', with the idea that others become curious about you. Modern {心憎|こころにく}い still means 'admirably clever'. The plan is to appear suddenly as an expert. こそ … からめ: the realis form of む closes the こそ.
めり: 'it seems', 'apparently'. Kenkō has heard this excuse many times.

notes.quote: かくいふ人、一芸もならひ得ることなし
notes.text: The verdict comes immediately and without pity. For anyone who studies Japanese and has never said a sentence out loud to a Japanese speaker: this section is about you.
{堅固|けんご} here means 'completely, utterly' (not modern 'solid'). かたほ: 'incomplete, unskilled'.
{骨|こつ}: 'knack, natural talent'. Modern コツ 'the knack (of doing something)' comes from this word.

notes.quote: 堪能の嗜まざるよりは
notes.text: {堪能|かんのう}: a gifted person. Modern Japanese reads the same kanji たんのう, 'skilled, fluent'. Kenkō's point: practice beats talent that does not practise.
{放埒|はうらつ}: 'doing as one likes'. The 1925 edition explains the image: a horse let out of its fence (埒).
